changed.old_text: Sartre called it 'the first principle of existentialism': existence precedes essence. Your 'essence' would be a fixed nature that decides who you are; existentialists say we are not born with one. A person first 'turns up' and only afterwards defines himself, through choices made as life unfolds. Hard facts still limit us, such as our body and the time and place we live in. But we can question those facts, give them meaning and decide what to do with them. A strong craving, for example, does not force me to act on it.
changed.new_text: Sartre called it 'the first principle of existentialism': existence precedes essence. Your 'essence' would be a fixed nature that decides who you are; existentialists say we are not born with one. A person first 'turns up' and only afterwards defines himself, through choices made as life unfolds. How free are we, then? Early Sartre called our freedom 'absolute'. Later, he and others such as Beauvoir stressed that our circumstances, such as our body and our time and place, limit it. But we can still question those limits, give them meaning and decide what to do with them. A strong craving, for example, does not force me to act on it.

Three thinkers answered it differently: | Nietzsche summed up the crisis as 'God is dead': not that God literally died, but that belief in the Christian God had become unbelievable, so the morality built on it was set to collapse. His answer: create your own values. | Camus called our situation 'the absurd', the clash between our 'wild longing for clarity' and 'the unreasonable silence of the world'. If life has no meaning, he asked, is it still worth living, or is suicide the answer? He said it is worth living: reject suicide and false hope, and live fully aware. | Beauvoir said existence is not absurd, since that would mean it can never be given a meaning. It is 'ambiguous': 'its meaning is never fixed', so we keep making it.

changed.old_text: But there is a better way. Beauvoir's 'authentic love' nurtures the other person's freedom instead of possessing them. Why does my freedom need yours? If I see freedom as the core of what I am, I must see it as the core of others too, and help them realise it. As Sartre put it, in wanting freedom 'we discover that it depends entirely on the freedom of others'.
changed.new_text: But there is a better way. Beauvoir's 'authentic love' nurtures the other person's freedom instead of possessing them. Why does my freedom need yours? We see ourselves through each other's eyes, so my freedom is bound up with yours. That is why we must help free each other, so that each of us can create ourselves. As Sartre put it, in wanting freedom 'we discover that it depends entirely on the freedom of others'.

changed.old_text: Sartre's own example is a student of his in wartime France, who came to him for advice. He could: | go to England and join the Free French Forces, to avenge his brother, killed in the German offensive of 1940, or | stay with his mother, who lived only for him. || But choosing an adviser, Sartre said, is already a choice: you more or less know what they will say. His only reply was 'You are free, therefore choose, that is to say, invent.' One way to use his point: before your next hard choice, ask yourself why you picked the person you are asking, and what you already expect them to say.
